title: The verse at Sill Hall
public_context: Community archives sometimes preserve local music through oral histories, program cards, and recordings made at public events. The following fictional file comes from an archive collection about a singing group and a benefit performance. Its setting and document type are familiar to readers of community music histories.
source_title: Morrow Choral Union oral-history transcript and archive sleeve
source_text:
The community archive filed this transcript under Flood Benefit, although Ansel Roe begins by saying he remembers a song better than he remembers the fundraiser's receipts. The interview took place on 12 May 2002. Roe says he sang tenor in the Morrow Choral Union as a young deckhand. A catalog card lists Net-Menders' Round in the program at Sill Hall's 1964 benefit, but the card gives no verse count.

Roe remembers the song as a leader's line answered by a group of singers. He says Maura Fen began alone, then the women at the long table answered on the last two words. He places the accordion under the response, holding one note until the group released it. “We had no conductor's baton,” he says, “only Maura's hand and the table keeping time.” The transcript preserves his phrasing rather than correcting it to match later choir terminology.

At the second verse, Roe recalls, a table of net-menders answered before Maura lifted her hand. The singers held the final note while Pat Deller tapped the music stand twice, and Maura took the next line after the room quieted. Roe says, “We did not sing the third verse that night.” He recalls no argument about the early response; the group finished the song and stayed for the next item on the benefit card.

A borrowed tape machine was switched on after the first verse because its operator had been sent to collect a fresh reel. The surviving cassette therefore begins with the second verse. When archive staff played it for Roe, he recognized his lower harmony under the answer but did not identify the voice that begins the recording. He also says he never saw a complete written score for the song, only two lyric sheets kept beside the accordion case.

The file includes a later interview with hall steward Leda Mor, who remembers the union beginning with a chorus rather than Maura singing alone. Mor was standing near the door to admit late guests, while Roe was on the platform. Neither interview names a set list beyond the title on the card. The archive sleeve lists one cassette and two handwritten sheets; no page count is given for either sheet.

Roe asks the interviewer not to call the early answer a new arrangement. He says the table may have heard Maura's breath, or may simply have known the song well. After the interview, the archivist returned the cassette to its paper sleeve and wrote both recollections on the same catalog card, leaving the title in its original ink.
structure_tags: retrospective testimony contrasted with a partial recording
two witnesses recall different opening forms
informal audience response within a performed song
authoring_note: This oral-history dossier preserves attributed memories, one incomplete recording, and a catalog description without elevating testimony into independently verified event facts.

supported_claims.claim: The archive catalog card lists Net-Menders' Round in the program for Sill Hall's 1964 benefit.
evidence: A catalog card lists Net-Menders' Round in the program at Sill Hall's 1964 benefit, but the card gives no verse count.

supported_claims.claim: Roe remembers the song opening with Maura alone and then a group response.
evidence: He says Maura Fen began alone, then the women at the long table answered on the last two words.

supported_claims.claim: Roe recalls an early response, a held note, two taps by Pat, and Maura's next line after the room quieted.
evidence: At the second verse, Roe recalls, a table of net-menders answered before Maura lifted her hand. The singers held the final note while Pat Deller tapped the music stand twice, and Maura took the next line after the room quieted.

supported_claims.claim: Roe says the group completed the song and stayed for the next benefit item.
evidence: Roe says, “We did not sing the third verse that night.” He recalls no argument about the early response; the group finished the song and stayed for the next item on the benefit card.

supported_claims.claim: The surviving cassette starts with the second verse because the machine was turned on after the first.
evidence: A borrowed tape machine was switched on after the first verse because its operator had been sent to collect a fresh reel. The surviving cassette therefore begins with the second verse.

supported_claims.claim: Mor remembers a chorus opening, unlike Roe's memory of Maura beginning alone.
evidence: The file includes a later interview with hall steward Leda Mor, who remembers the union beginning with a chorus rather than Maura singing alone.

explicit_negatives.claim: Roe says the group did not sing the third verse that night.
evidence: Roe says, “We did not sing the third verse that night.”

explicit_negatives.claim: Roe says he never saw a complete written score for the song.
evidence: He also says he never saw a complete written score for the song, only two lyric sheets kept beside the accordion case.

licensed_inferences.claim: Roe's remembered response timing was handled within the song rather than by stopping the performance.
licensed_inferences.rationale: His account describes a held note and two taps followed by Maura's next line, then says the group finished the song; it does not establish the exact tempo or every singer's action.

licensed_inferences.claim: The file does not reconcile the witnesses' different memories of the opening.
licensed_inferences.rationale: Roe recalls a solo opening while Mor remembers a chorus, and neither account is independently adjudicated in the file.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: Who developed the call-and-response form of Net-Menders' Round?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: How did Maura Fen create the call-and-response form of Net-Menders' Round?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: Maura Fen created the call-and-response form of Net-Menders' Round.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: Roe describes Maura's role in one remembered performance but does not identify who developed the song form.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: Did the union use the early audience response in later performances?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: How did the union keep the net-menders' early response in later performances?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: The union kept the net-menders' early response in later performances.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The file contains one remembered event and no later performance account or set list.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: What words were sung in the first verse on the cassette night?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: What was the river-gate line in the first verse?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: The first verse included a line naming the river gate.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The cassette begins after the first verse, and the catalog card and interviews do not supply its wording.

consistency_questions.question: What does Roe's account say happened when the audience response came early?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: Roe remembers Maura leading the response form, then a table answering early. The singers held a note while Pat tapped twice; Maura continued after the room quieted, and Roe says they omitted the third verse and finished the song.

consistency_questions.question: How do the catalog, cassette, and two interviews differ in what they can establish?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The card lists the song in the benefit program, the cassette starts only at verse two, Roe recalls a solo opening, and Mor recalls a chorus opening. The file does not resolve which memory is correct or provide the missing first verse.
